stages.title: Trade restrictions: dumping and non-tariff barriers
stages.sub: Explain why governments act against dumping, and recognise non-tariff barriers to trade.

steps.q: A foreign steel firm sells steel in your country for less than it cost to make. Is this normal profit-seeking behaviour, or something else?
steps.right: Something else, it is selling at a loss on purpose
steps.wrong: Normal profit-seeking, just at a low price
steps.hint: Would a firm normally choose to sell for less than production cost?
steps.pre: Selling deliberately for less than it costs to produce is

steps.q: If the foreign steel firm keeps undercutting local steelmakers this way, what is likely to happen to those local firms?
steps.right: They lose customers and may shut down
steps.wrong: They are unaffected, since prices vary anyway
steps.hint: Local firms cannot sell at a loss for long. What happens to their sales?

steps.q: Given that local firms could be driven out by this below-cost selling, why might a government step in and restrict these imports?
steps.right: To stop unfairly cheap imports damaging domestic firms
steps.wrong: To raise extra tax revenue from imports
steps.hint: Think about what problem the government is trying to fix here, not about collecting money.

steps.q: Instead of taxing the steel at the border, the government simply says only 1,000 tonnes of foreign steel may enter this year. Does this work by adding a tax, or by limiting the amount allowed in?
steps.right: By limiting the amount allowed in, with no tax
steps.wrong: By adding a tax on each tonne imported
steps.hint: Is a price being added here, or is a physical limit being set?

steps.q: Quotas, safety regulations, product standards and outright bans on certain goods all restrict trade without ever taxing anything. What general name covers all of these?
steps.right: Non-tax barriers based on rules and limits
steps.hint: None of these involve a price added at the border. What do they rely on instead?
